newsitem.title: NAMIBIA: Namibia still fighting for equality seven years on.
newsitem.headline: Namibia still fighting for equality seven years on.

text.p: Namibia celebrated seven years of independence at the weekend but despite the stability the country has achieved, President Sam Nujoma says he is still fighting problems inherited from the South African apartheid administration.

"I call it the second phase of the struggle, the struggle for economic development and empowerment of our people to be able to exploit the natural resources for the benefit of all," Nujoma told Reuters in an interview.

Formerly known as South West Africa, Namibia was ruled by South Africa for 75 years. Nujoma led the South West Africa People's Organisation (SWAPO), which began a guerrilla war to end South African rule in 1966.
He admits that poverty is visible and that the country has enormous problems, but says he believes mineral-rich Namibia can succeed.

"To eradicate poverty, ignorance and disease, and to narrow the disparity between the haves and have-nots, we have found that we have to concentrate on education and training for our people at all levels, right from kindergarten to university."
His statement is borne out by successive budgets which have placed the main spending priority on education and health.

"Without an educated and trained workforce one can't do anything. We have many resources which could be exploited quickly to eradicate poverty, but as it is we are sitting on top of that wealth," the president said.
The Namibian economy is dependent of foreign skilled labour.
According to the Namibian Economic Policy Research Unit (NEPRU), an estimated 18.1 percent of senior officials and 13.9 percent of professionals are recruited outside the country.
Nujoma says his government must realistically take a long-term view on the time needed before skilled Namibians can take over.

For a country with huge unemployment, this is not easy to swallow. NEPRU, in a paper on the situation seven years after independence, said the combined rate of unemployment and underemployment is as high as 60 percent of the labour force.
Nujoma backed his agriculture minister Helmut Angula in a proposal to introduce compulsory national service as a way to train and occupy the nation's youth, saying:
"It's a good idea. It certainly exists in many countries and it would provide young people with some skills."
Apart from this scheme, Nujoma is confident that given time and an improvement in the long-suffering areas of agriculture and fisheries, the unemployment problem can be addressed.

"Unfortunately during the past two years we had devastating drought and we also lost our fish stocks. So we have those natural disasters, and we have to work within the framework of these difficulties. But we have the capacity and we have the commitment and we will succeed."
Another way in which the government is trying to address inequality is through land redistribution, a policy that is high on the political agenda. But progress has been slow, as Nujoma acknowledges.
"We have succeeded to resettle some of our people, but that is not enough. We still have to buy more land and resettle the people, but it takes time too."
He does however reject a policy of buying land against the will of the occupier, stressing that the government will follow the principle of "willing seller, willing buyer".

While Nujoma has produced one of the most democratic administrations in Africa, opposition parties criticise him for failing to improve the lives of Namibians, which could harm his party in elections scheduled for 1998.
